quote: Is there any way on the title but you and your wife? Or sorry. Just you?
stewart_read: Craig discloses he had a prior company (Fluent Solar) for the existing system. The rep never probes what happened with that company, why it ended, or whether it's relevant to the removal request — competitive/relationship context a closer or specialist would want.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged this irrelevant since the call isn't heading toward a new install, so probing would waste time on a call already drifting off standard script.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to ask one quick follow-up ('what happened with Fluent Solar?') when a prior provider is named — costs seconds, gives real context for routing the removal request correctly.

quote: Is she she looking into solar too?
stewart_read: Mary Anne, the actual title-holder/homeowner, is not on the call. Instead of treating this as a co-owner-inclusion moment (schema requires the title co-owner be part of the appointment), the rep asks a generic interest question and drops it entirely once Craig says they already have panels. This is more consequential than a standard spouse-objection miss because Mary Anne owns the home outright and Craig is not even the titleholder.
alternative_hypothesis: Because the call never reaches an appointment-setting stage, there was no concrete appointment to include Mary Anne in — so the omission may be moot given how the call ultimately ends.
coaching_implication: Any time the rep learns someone other than the person on the phone holds title, that person's inclusion should be flagged immediately for any future appointment, regardless of where the call ends up. Flag this as a standing habit gap, not just a one-call miss.

quote: Were you looking for, like, an add on?
stewart_read: Craig's answer ('we need them removed and reinstalled until the home reno is finished') is a scenario orphaned_flow doesn't fully cover — it's not a lease/PPA DQ, not an 'add-on' interest, and not a broken-system case. It's a temporary removal-for-renovation request. The rep's one qualifying question here doesn't map onto any of orphaned_flow's four listed checks (own/lease, prior company, panel size, system working), and the rep never asks the one relevant orphaned_flow item that WOULD apply — whether the current system is working — before pivoting into the standard new-design pitch.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have correctly sensed this doesn't fit the DQ checklist and moved past it quickly rather than force an irrelevant script item — a defensible read given the schema itself has no removal/reinstall category.
coaching_implication: This is a genuine schema gap Ion needs to close (no removal-only flow exists), but in the interim the rep should escalate ('let me check with my team on how we handle removal-only requests') rather than defaulting to the standard design pitch that visibly frustrates the customer three separate times afterward.

quote: Yeah. Well so we have a program. It's called the the bill swap.
stewart_read: Immediately after Craig explicitly says he isn't looking to buy panels, the rep launches into the full bill-swap pitch anyway — premature program-selling into a customer who has already signaled it doesn't apply to him.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have been trying to re-engage Craig's curiosity by showing potential value, which briefly worked ('I'm curious to hear more' at 02:53) before collapsing when the new-panels assumption resurfaced.
coaching_implication: The brief spark of interest at 02:53 shows the pitch itself wasn't the problem — the problem was not immediately clarifying that this specific customer's situation (removal/reinstall, no new panels) doesn't require the standard pitch at all. Coach the rep to answer the customer's stated need BEFORE pitching.

quote: Yeah. I understand. But you're trying to sell me new panels, and that's not what I need.
stewart_read: This is the clearest statement of the mismatch in the whole call. The rep's response ('No you don't have to pay for the panels at all') answers a cost objection that was never raised — Craig's objection is about wanting the service at all, not the price of new panels.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have genuinely misheard 'that's not what I need' as a cost concern given how often cost objections come up on these calls, rather than a scope mismatch.
coaching_implication: When a customer says a specific phrase like 'that's not what I need,' the rep should repeat it back and directly resolve the mismatch ('understood — you don't want new panels, you want removal only') before continuing, rather than defaulting to a generic cost rebuttal.

quote: Man, I'm I'm sorry. I'm actually good. I'm I'm this isn't what I'm looking for. I appreciate your help.
stewart_read: The call ends with no resolution and no next step. The rep never gave Craig a direct yes/no on whether Ion offers standalone removal service, so Craig disengages politely rather than the rep either booking a specialist call or cleanly closing the file.
coaching_implication: Even on a call the rep can't close, the rep should end with either a direct answer ('let me find out and call you back') or a clean close, not let the customer be the one to end the mismatch.
